In a curious twist of timing and irony, Michael Lamar, a 44-year-old Pennsylvania native who bears a striking resemblance to President Barack Obama, has landed a starring role in a Turkish bank commercial—one that hit airwaves just days before Obama's real-life visit to the country. The advertisement, produced for Garanti Bank, capitalizes on Lamar's uncanny likeness to the American president to promote the bank's new low-interest loan offerings.

The commercial takes a lighthearted approach, featuring Lamar's Obama character enthusiastically praising Garanti Bank's economic stimulus package. In a moment clearly designed for comedic effect, the faux-Obama expresses a wistful desire that the United States had access to a similar program—a playful jab at America's own economic struggles, delivered by a stand-in for the very president tasked with solving them.

According to Can Celikbilek, the advertising copywriter behind the campaign, the choice to feature an Obama impersonator was far from arbitrary. Celikbilek explained that Obama was selected specifically because of what he represents: a symbol of hope, both within the United States and around the world. Unlike previous American presidents, Obama's image carries a universal resonance that made him the ideal figure to anchor a campaign about financial optimism and recovery, even in a foreign market like Turkey.

What makes Lamar's involvement particularly poignant, however, is the personal story behind his casting. Just months before landing this unexpected acting gig, Lamar had been laid off from JP Morgan Chase Bank in January 2009, following an 18-year career with the company. His job loss made him one of countless casualties of the very economic crisis that the commercial's storyline addresses—a crisis that Obama, the man Lamar now portrays, has been working to resolve. The parallel between actor and character is almost too fitting: a man who lost his livelihood in the financial meltdown now plays the leader trying to fix it.

For Lamar, this ironic turn of events may prove to be a silver lining. Having found himself unexpectedly unemployed after nearly two decades in banking, this commercial opportunity has opened an unforeseen door. With his resemblance to the president now proven marketable, Lamar is considering the possibility of building a new career as a professional Obama impersonator—a path that could offer him steady work and financial stability for his family during uncertain economic times.

In a curious twist of global economics and marketing savvy, Garanti Bank, one of Turkey's largest financial institutions, has launched an eye-catching nationwide advertising campaign featuring an American man who bears a striking resemblance to President Barack Obama. The campaign, designed to promote the bank's new low-interest loan stimulus package, comes at a particularly symbolic moment: just ahead of President Obama's own visit to Turkey, a trip being closely watched as part of his broader outreach to the Muslim world and European allies.

The face of the campaign is Michael Lamar, an American man who until recently worked for JP Morgan Chase—one of the very financial institutions at the center of the global economic meltdown. Lamar was laid off from his position as the crisis deepened, joining the ranks of thousands of displaced workers whose jobs evaporated amid the banking sector's turmoil. In an unexpected turn of fate, however, his uncanny physical resemblance to the American president has opened up a new and unlikely career path: professional Obama impersonation.

Garanti Bank's marketing team seized upon this resemblance to craft advertisements that tap into the widespread optimism and global fascination surrounding Obama's presidency. Since taking office, Obama has become something of an international symbol—a figure representing hope, change, and the possibility of economic renewal, themes that resonate deeply with consumers still reeling from the financial crisis. By featuring a man who looks remarkably like the American leader, the bank aims to associate its loan products with these same feelings of optimism and forward momentum, encouraging Turkish citizens to take advantage of favorable borrowing rates to stimulate personal and business spending.

The irony of the situation has not been lost on observers. Lamar, a direct casualty of the very economic collapse triggered in part by practices at major financial institutions like his former employer, has found a strange form of professional redemption by capitalizing on the image of the man now tasked with steering the global economy back to stability. What began as a personal setback—the loss of a stable banking career—has transformed into a new, if unconventional, livelihood: standing in for the President of the United States in commercial advertisements thousands of miles from Washington.

The campaign's timing is especially notable given the broader diplomatic context. Obama's visit to Turkey was seen as a significant gesture, part of his administration's efforts to strengthen ties with the Muslim world and to position Turkey as a bridge between East and West. The country, a NATO member with a majority Muslim population and aspirations for European Union membership, held particular symbolic importance for the new administration's foreign policy outreach.

Against this backdrop, Garanti's advertising strategy cleverly merges commercial interest with cultural and political symbolism. By using an Obama look-alike to sell financial products, the bank taps into the global cachet of the American president's brand of hope and change, repurposing it for domestic economic ends—encouraging Turkish consumers and businesses to borrow, spend, and invest at a moment when confidence in financial institutions remains fragile worldwide.

For Michael Lamar, the experience represents an unlikely silver lining amid personal financial hardship. Having lost his job in the very industry blamed for triggering the global downturn, he now finds himself, quite literally, playing the part of the man positioned to lead the world out of that same crisis—a strange but fitting metaphor for the unpredictable ways in which economic upheaval can reshape individual lives and unexpected opportunities can emerge from financial ruin.

# CNN Reports from Istanbul: A City Bridging Continents

Istanbul, Turkey's largest and most culturally significant city, has frequently been featured in CNN's international news coverage as a critical hub connecting Europe and Asia. Straddling the Bosphorus Strait, this historic metropolis serves as a focal point for stories ranging from geopolitics to culture, economics, and travel.

## A Strategic Location

CNN correspondents often highlight Istanbul's unique geographic position when reporting on Middle Eastern and European affairs. As the only city in the world situated on two continents, Istanbul provides a natural backdrop for discussions about East-West relations, trade routes, and diplomatic negotiations. Its proximity to conflict zones and its role in refugee movements have made it a frequent dateline for CNN's international correspondents covering regional crises.

## Political and Economic Coverage

Turkey's political landscape, including its relationship with NATO, the European Union, and neighboring countries, regularly draws CNN's attention. Istanbul, as the country's economic engine and most populous city, often serves as the setting for reports on Turkish elections, economic policy, and social movements. The city's business district and financial markets provide context for stories about Turkey's broader economic trajectory.

## Cultural and Historical Significance

Beyond hard news, CNN Travel and lifestyle segments frequently showcase Istanbul's rich cultural heritage. The Hagia Sophia, Blue Mosque, Grand Bazaar, and the vibrant neighborhoods along the Bosphorus offer compelling visual storytelling opportunities. These features often explore the city's Byzantine and Ottoman history alongside its modern transformation into a global tourist destination and creative hub.

## A City of Contrasts

What makes Istanbul particularly compelling for international media coverage is its embodiment of contrasts—ancient and modern, secular and religious, Eastern and Western influences all converging in a single metropolis. This complexity ensures that Istanbul remains a recurring subject in global news narratives, offering CNN and other outlets endless angles for exploring Turkey's evolving identity on the world stage.

Istanbul's continued relevance in international media reflects its enduring importance not just to Turkey, but to broader conversations about global politics, culture, and connectivity between East and West.

# Turkish Bank Sparks Controversy With Obama Look-Alike in Loan Advertisement

**ISTANBUL** — A Turkish bank has ignited a social media firestorm and diplomatic eyebrow-raising after releasing a television commercial featuring an actor bearing a striking resemblance to former U.S. President Barack Obama, using his likeness to promote low-interest personal loans.

The advertisement, which began airing on Turkish television networks and social media platforms this week, shows the Obama look-alike in a scene reminiscent of a presidential address, standing behind a podium adorned with the bank's logo before pivoting to enthusiastically endorse the institution's new loan packages.

"Yes, you can... afford that dream home," the actor says in the ad, delivering a play on Obama's famous 2008 campaign slogan "Yes We Can," before breaking into a grin and gesturing toward on-screen text detailing interest rates.

## Social Media Reaction Swift and Divided

The commercial quickly went viral, amassing millions of views across Twitter, Instagram, and TikTok within 48 hours. Reactions have been sharply divided, with some users finding the ad humorous and clever, while others have called it tasteless and potentially legally problematic.

"This is either brilliant marketing or a lawsuit waiting to happen," one Twitter user wrote in a post that garnered over 50,000 likes.

Media law experts have weighed in on the murky legal territory surrounding the use of political figures' likenesses in foreign advertising markets.

"Right of publicity laws vary dramatically from country to country," said Elena Marsh, a media and entertainment attorney based in Los Angeles. "In the United States, using a look-alike in a way that implies endorsement without consent could open a company up to significant legal liability. Whether those protections extend to a Turkish company running ads primarily for a domestic audience is a much more complicated question."

## Bank Defends Campaign as Satire

The bank, whose name is being withheld pending official response, released a statement Thursday defending the advertisement as clearly satirical entertainment rather than a genuine implication of endorsement.

"Our campaign is intended as lighthearted commentary and wordplay, not to suggest any real affiliation with or endorsement from President Obama," the statement read. "We have full confidence our audience understands the humorous intent behind the advertisement."

The bank did not respond to questions about whether they had sought any form of legal clearance before producing the commercial.

## Obama's Team Has Not Commented

Representatives for the former president have not yet issued a public statement regarding the commercial. CNN has reached out to Obama's office for comment.

This is not the first time Obama's likeness has been used commercially without his direct involvement. Look-alikes and impersonators have appeared in various forms of media and advertising globally in the years since he left office, though few have generated the level of attention this Turkish campaign has received.

Legal analysts note that pursuing international claims over likeness rights can be exceedingly difficult and costly, meaning many such cases never proceed beyond public complaint or informal cease-and-desist requests.

## Broader Questions About Global Advertising Norms

The controversy has reignited discussion about the use of political figures' images in international markets, where regulations around celebrity likeness and political figure endorsement can differ substantially from U.S. standards.

Turkey's advertising regulatory body has not indicated whether it plans to review the commercial, and it remains unclear whether the ad will continue airing amid the growing attention.

As of publication, the commercial remains active across the bank's official social media channels, continuing to draw commentary from viewers both amused and unsettled by its unconventional approach to financial marketing.

*CNN has reached out to the Turkish bank for additional comment and will update this story as more information becomes available.*

# The Impersonator: How One Man Found a Second Act as Obama's Double

*A feature story*

---

The banquet hall in Kuala Lumpur was humming with pre-event chatter when Dwayne Reed slipped through a side door, adjusted his tie, and became someone else.

It wasn't a costume, exactly. Reed didn't wear a mask or prosthetics. He didn't need to. The resemblance had always been there—the height, the ears, the particular way his smile spread slowly across his face before fully arriving. What he'd learned to do, over three years of trial and error, was inhabit the rest: the measured cadence of speech, the thoughtful pause before answering a question, the slight tilt of the head that suggested careful consideration.

"Ladies and gentlemen," the emcee announced in accented English, "please welcome... the President of the United States."

The room erupted. Phones rose like a field of small moons. And Dwayne Reed, a fifty-two-year-old man who once analyzed mortgage-backed securities in a glass tower in Charlotte, North Carolina, walked out to thunderous applause eight thousand miles from home.

---

## The Fall

Reed doesn't romanticize what happened in 2009. He lost his job the way thousands of people did—suddenly, impersonally, via a mass email and a box for his belongings. Fifteen years at the bank, a solid title, a mortgage of his own to worry about now. Then: nothing.

"I sent out over two hundred resumes," he said, sitting in a hotel lobby in Singapore during a break between corporate gigs. "I heard back from maybe twelve. The finance world had contracted so much that guys with my exact profile—mid-career, mid-level, expensive—we were the first ones cut and the last ones anyone wanted to hire back."

He tried other things. Insurance sales. A brief, unsuccessful stint flipping foreclosed properties with a cousin. Nothing stuck. The unemployment checks ran out. His marriage, already strained, didn't survive the stress.

It was his teenage daughter, of all people, who planted the seed. At a Halloween party in 2010, she'd suggested—half-joking—that he go as the president. "You literally look like him if he was, like, forty pounds heavier and had a receding hairline," she'd said, which was not entirely a compliment but also not entirely wrong.

He didn't think much of it until he stood in front of a mirror in a cheap suit, practiced the speech pattern he'd heard a thousand times on cable news, and felt something click.

## The Discovery

The first booking was small—a local business conference, $200, a request to "just say a few funny lines and take pictures." Reed almost turned it down. It felt beneath him, somehow, a former finance professional playing dress-up for cash.

But $200 was $200.

The gig went better than expected. The organizer, delighted, mentioned him to a colleague. That colleague ran an event company. Within six months, Reed had a manager—a former talent booker named Priya Chandrasekaran who saw something the domestic market wasn't fully capitalizing on.

"American look-alikes were a novelty in the U.S., sure, but overseas? Especially in parts of Asia and the Middle East where Obama was genuinely popular, where he represented something aspirational?" Chandrasekaran said by phone from her office in Mumbai. "Dwayne wasn't just a party trick. He was, in some strange way, an ambassador."

The first international booking was in Manila in 2011—a telecommunications company's anniversary gala. Reed remembers being paid more for that single appearance than he'd made in a month at the bank.

"I stood backstage and I thought, this is insane. This cannot be a real job," he said. "And then I walked out and three hundred people stood up and started cheering, and I thought—okay. Okay, maybe it can."

## The Work

It is, Reed insists, actual work—not the punchline people assume.

There's the physical maintenance: the diet to keep his weight in the right range, the haircut he gets every eleven days without fail, the way he's had to relearn how to gesture, how to laugh, how to *pause* before delivering a line for maximum effect. He's studied hundreds of hours of speeches and interviews, not to mimic exactly, but to internalize a rhythm.

There's the research: understanding the political and cultural context of wherever he's landed, so he doesn't accidentally step into a controversy. In some countries, the booking company has him avoid all political commentary entirely—he's there for photos, for the spectacle of proximity to power, not for opinions.

And there's the strange emotional labor of representing, however loosely, a real person with real politics, real flaws, real complexity—while flattening all of that into an evening's entertainment.

"I'm not an actor. I never trained for this," Reed said. "I had to become a student of a human being. Not to imitate him cruelly, but almost—I don't know—reverently? People wanted a piece of that hope they remembered feeling. My job was to hand it back to them for an hour."

He's worked corporate galas in Dubai, product launches in Jakarta, a bizarre wedding in Lagos where the bride's father insisted "Obama" give a toast. He's been paid to do essentially nothing but stand next to executives for photos, his presence alone worth the fee. He's had grown men weep upon shaking his hand, overwhelmed by some feeling he never fully understood but learned to hold space for.

The pay varies wildly—anywhere from a few hundred dollars for a local gig to five figures for major international corporate events, though Reed is cagey about exact numbers. "Enough," he said. "Enough that I bought a house outright. Enough that my daughter's tuition doesn't keep me up at night."

## The Complication

It hasn't been without controversy. Some critics—both American and international—have accused Reed of profiting off a reductive, sometimes uncomfortably close approximation of a Black public figure, a kind of modern minstrelsy dressed up in a nice suit. Reed has heard this critique many times and doesn't dismiss it entirely.

"I think about it," he said, quieter than before. "I've turned down gigs that felt wrong—places that wanted jokes I wasn't comfortable making, a "type" of appearance that felt like it was mocking rather than honoring. I try to walk a line. I don't always know if I walk it perfectly."

There have also been legal gray areas—countries with different standards around name and likeness rights, event companies that have used his image in advertising without full clarity on permissions. Chandrasekaran now handles contracts meticulously, but Reed admits the early years were murkier.

## The Second Act

These days, Reed splits his time between a home outside Charlotte and extensive travel—forty, sometimes fifty bookings a year across a dozen countries. He's diversified too, working occasionally as a public speaker about reinvention, about what happens when the career you built disappears overnight.

He doesn't know how long the demand will last. Obama left office years ago; cultural relevance fades. Reed has started thinking about what comes after this act too—maybe consulting for other look-alikes trying to break into international markets, maybe something else entirely.

But for now, there's still a market for the feeling he sells: nostalgia, aspiration, a strange global hunger for a moment in history that, for reasons Reed still doesn't fully understand, crossed oceans and outlasted the presidency itself.

"I lost everything in 2009," he said, standing to leave for his next event, adjusting his tie in the lobby mirror—an old habit that never really left him. "And what I found on the other side of that wasn't a return to what I had. It was something I never could have imagined asking for."

He paused, and there it was—the smile, spreading slow, arriving fully.

"Funny where you end up," he said, "when you stop trying to be exactly who you were."

---

counterfactuals.output:
# The Billboard That Tells a Bigger Story

ISTANBUL — Along the highways leading into Turkey's largest city, a new advertisement has begun appearing on billboards, catching the attention of commuters and sparking conversations in coffeehouses from Istanbul to Ankara. It doesn't sell soap or cars. Instead, it sells an idea: that America, once viewed with deep suspicion here, might be worth a second look.

The ad campaign, launched by a coalition aiming to improve U.S.-Turkey relations, prominently features President Obama—not as a foreign policy abstraction, but as a recognizable, almost familiar face. The choice is deliberate, and it is working precisely because of what came before.

## A Nation That Soured

To understand why an advertisement built around a single American politician makes sense in Turkey, one has to remember the depths from which U.S. favorability here had fallen. During the George W. Bush administration, American approval ratings in Turkey collapsed to some of the lowest levels recorded anywhere in the world—hovering in the single digits by some polling measures in the mid-2000s.

The Iraq War sat at the center of this collapse. Turkey, a NATO ally with a long and complicated history of cooperation with Washington, watched a war unfold on its southern border that many Turks viewed as reckless, destabilizing, and driven by American unilateralism. Turkish parliament's refusal in 2003 to allow U.S. troops to use Turkish territory as a staging ground for the invasion of Iraq marked a symbolic break—one that lingered in public sentiment long after the vote itself.

Adding to the resentment was a perception, widely shared across the Turkish political spectrum, that Washington paid insufficient attention to Turkish concerns about Kurdish separatism and cross-border security. The sense of being taken for granted—of being useful to America only when convenient—hardened into something closer to distrust.

## Enter Obama

Obama's rise to the presidency, and particularly his early outreach to the Muslim world, shifted this dynamic in ways that pollsters and diplomats alike found notable. His 2009 visit to Turkey, one of his first foreign trips as president, was widely covered and well received. He spoke in Ankara about mutual respect, framed American engagement with the Muslim world in less adversarial terms, and made a point of visiting Hagia Sophia and other symbolic sites—gestures that read, to many Turks, as an acknowledgment long overdue.

The shift in approval numbers that followed was not universal or permanent, but it was real. Where Bush-era polling had shown overwhelming disapproval of the United States, Obama's personal favorability—separate from and often higher than approval of American policy generally—gave advertisers and diplomats alike a new asset to work with.

## Selling a Relationship, Not Just a Politician

This is the terrain the new billboard campaign is navigating. By centering Obama rather than abstract references to "America" or "partnership," the campaign's designers appear to understand something important about how public opinion actually functions: people respond to faces and personalities more readily than to institutions or policies.

Critics, of course, will point out the risk in this approach. Personal popularity is not policy alignment, and goodwill generated by rhetoric and symbolic visits can evaporate quickly if not backed by substantive shifts in how the two countries cooperate on issues like Iraq, Syria, or Kurdish autonomy. A president's charisma is not a permanent asset; it is, at best, a bridge.

But bridges matter. And for a relationship that just a few years ago seemed to be fraying past the point of easy repair, an advertisement willing to put a smiling, recognizable American face on a Turkish billboard represents something more than marketing. It represents a bet—that the goodwill generated by one presidency's tone and rhetoric can be leveraged into something more durable, before the moment passes and old suspicions reassert themselves.

Whether that bet pays off remains, as ever, a question for history rather than advertising executives. But for now, at least, the billboards are up—and people are looking.

# Turkish Ad Agency Sparks Debate with Obama Look-Alike Casting Call

**ISTANBUL, Turkey** — A Turkish advertising agency has set social media abuzz after announcing a casting call for an actor bearing a striking resemblance to U.S. President Barack Obama, intended for use in an upcoming bank commercial.

The agency, based in Istanbul, confirmed this week that it is seeking a look-alike to appear in a series of television spots for a domestic banking chain, though details about the specific campaign concept remain under wraps. Casting directors say they've already received dozens of submissions from hopeful actors across Turkey.

"We wanted someone who embodies a sense of trust, change, and forward-thinking — qualities associated with Obama's image worldwide," said one agency representative, who declined to be named citing company policy. "The response has been overwhelming."

The move has reignited conversations among everyday Turks about their perceptions of American leadership, with many drawing sharp contrasts between Obama and his predecessor, George W. Bush.

"Obama represents something different for us," said Mehmet Yildiz, a 34-year-old shop owner in Istanbul's Beyoglu district. "Under Bush, there was so much tension, especially with the wars in the region. Obama feels like he listens more, like he wants to build bridges rather than walls."

Others echoed similar sentiments, pointing to Obama's early outreach to the Muslim world, including his high-profile visit to Turkey in April 2009 — one of his first foreign trips as president.

"When Obama came here and spoke about mutual respect between America and the Muslim world, it meant something," said Ayse Demir, a university student in Ankara. "Bush never gave us that impression. It always felt like 'us versus them' during his years."

Not everyone, however, sees the casting decision as purely political. Some locals expressed amusement at the novelty of the campaign, noting that celebrity and political look-alikes have long been a staple of global advertising.

"Honestly, I just think it's funny," laughed Kemal Aydin, a taxi driver. "Whether it's Obama or Bush or anyone else, using a look-alike is just a marketing trick to grab attention. But sure, if you're going to copy a foreign leader, better Obama than Bush — at least people will smile when they see him."

Still, the choice underscores broader public opinion trends in Turkey, where polling in recent years has shown a marked improvement in favorability toward the United States following Obama's election, a shift often attributed to his rhetoric on diplomacy and religious tolerance.

The bank has not yet released details on when the commercial will air, but the casting call alone has already generated headlines — and no shortage of debate over what, exactly, an Obama look-alike says about Turkish perceptions of American power, policy, and personality.

# From Wall Street to the Spotlight: How a Laid-Off Banker Found New Purpose as an Obama Look-Alike

When corporate restructuring cost him his position at JPMorgan Chase, few could have predicted the unusual career pivot that awaited him. Today, this former financial services employee has built a surprising second act—capitalizing on his uncanny resemblance to former President Barack Obama to launch a career as a professional celebrity impersonator.

## An Unexpected Career Change

Like thousands of other financial sector workers affected by layoffs and corporate restructuring in recent years, our subject found himself suddenly unemployed after years of steady work in banking. Rather than immediately pursuing another position in finance, he decided to explore an opportunity that had followed him for years: strangers constantly stopping him to remark on his striking resemblance to the 44th President of the United States.

What began as an occasional joke among colleagues and friends has transformed into a legitimate business venture. He now works with talent agencies specializing in celebrity look-alikes, booking appearances for corporate events, private parties, promotional campaigns, and entertainment productions worldwide.

## Going International

His new career has taken him far beyond the New York metropolitan area where he once commuted to a Wall Street office. International clients—particularly in regions where Obama remains a globally recognizable figure—have flown him to events across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. Corporate conferences, television commercials, and themed parties have all called upon his services, allowing him to experience a level of international travel his previous career never afforded him.

Event organizers value the novelty and entertainment factor he brings, often incorporating him into themed events, comedy sketches, or simply as a photo opportunity for attendees. The appearances typically involve costume styling, coaching on mannerisms, and sometimes scripted routines that play into the persona.

## The Irony Isn't Lost on Him

Perhaps the most striking element of this story is the irony he readily acknowledges: transitioning from the world of high finance—an industry Obama's administration both bailed out and later regulated more strictly following the 2008 financial crisis—to literally embodying the former president for a living.

"There's something almost poetic about it," he has reflected in interviews about his career change. The same political figure whose administration reshaped banking regulations through Dodd-Frank now indirectly provides his livelihood through impersonation work. The economic policies and financial oversight that defined Obama's presidency stand in stark contrast to the entertainment industry where his lookalike now finds success.

## Finding Silver Linings

Beyond the financial benefits, he has spoken about the personal fulfillment this unexpected path has provided. Where corporate banking offered stability but perhaps limited personal expression, his new career allows for creativity, travel, and constant social interaction—elements he says were missing from his previous cubicle-based existence.

The transition also speaks to broader themes many displaced workers face: the necessity of reinvention, the value of unexpected skills or attributes, and the resilience required to pivot careers, sometimes into entirely unforeseen territories.

## A Modern Career Story

This banker-turned-lookalike's journey reflects a growing trend in the gig economy, where individuals leverage unique personal attributes—whether physical resemblance, specialized skills, or unconventional talents—into viable income streams. His story serves as both an entertaining anecdote and a broader commentary on economic resilience in an unpredictable job market.

While he may joke about the ironic twist his career has taken, there's no denying that his ability to adapt, embrace an unusual opportunity, and build a global business around it demonstrates the kind of resourcefulness that transcends any single industry—financial or otherwise.

*This story highlights the increasingly common phenomenon of career reinvention following corporate layoffs, showcasing how unexpected personal traits can become valuable professional assets in today's diverse entertainment marketplace.*
